The fix-it version is actually the more workable of the two. "Who do we call, should we talk to the landlord" — that's a man who's engaged and scared and reaching for the only tool in the box. It's not contempt, and it's not him re-filing you. It's him missing the point in a way you can redirect in the moment: "Stop. Not tonight. I don't need a plan, I need you to hear it."

The quiet-and-weird version is the one that would hurt, because silence is a screen and you'd project your worst story onto it. But notice: you're predicting both from zero data. You've never given him the sentence, so you've never seen what he does with it. The prediction is coming from the fear, not from him.

Here's the thing that might actually help — you said you can't picture him sitting with it. So don't leave "sitting with it" undefined. Tell him what it looks like. "I need you to say something like 'that sounds really hard' and then not solve it tonight." Give him the script. A fixer can follow a script; he just can't invent one.

What would you want him to actually say? Not the perfect thing — the good-enough thing.
